title: Human overpopulation

definition.text: The idea that human populations may grow too large to be supported by their environment or resources over the long term.

facts.text: Since 1804 world population has grown from 1 billion to 8 billion thanks to medical advances and higher farm productivity.
Annual population growth peaked at 2.1% in 1968 and has since dropped to 1.1%; the UN projects a peak of about 10.4 billion in the 2080s.
The IPCC found GDP per person and population growth were the strongest drivers of fossil CO2 emissions in 2010–2019, raising emissions about 2.3% and 1.2% a year respectively.
Proponents say overpopulation, population growth and overconsumption together are the main drivers of human-caused environmental problems such as climate change.
Thomas Malthus predicted in the early 19th century that population would outgrow the resources a finite amount of land can supply.
Poverty and infant mortality have declined over 200 years of population growth, and the predicted 'population explosion' did not happen as growth slowed.
Critics call the concept racist because population control often targets the Global South rather than overconsumption in the Global North.

contested_note: Whether overpopulation is a real cause of environmental problems, rather than consumption or technology, is strongly disputed.

definition.text: Attempts to estimate the largest human population the Earth can support.

facts.text: A 2004 meta-analysis of 69 studies found an average predicted maximum of 7.7 billion people, with bounds of 0.65 and 98 billion.
A 2012 UN report summarized 65 estimates of the maximum sustainable population; the most common was 8 billion.
Advocates of a smaller population put forward much lower figures, such as Paul Ehrlich's optimum of 1.5 to 2 billion.

definition.text: Proposals to stabilize and then gradually reduce human numbers as a response to overpopulation.

facts.text: Suggested approaches include better access to contraception and sex education, and lower infant mortality so parents need fewer children.
Educating and empowering women and giving access to family planning have a demonstrated effect in lowering birthrates.
Nearly 40% of pregnancies worldwide are unintended, some 80 million a year.
Coercive measures such as China's one-child policy and compulsory sterilization have drawn strong criticism.

title: I = PAT

definition.text: A formula stating that human impact on the environment (I) is the product of population (P), affluence (A) and technology (T).

facts.text: It was developed in 1970 during a debate between Barry Commoner, Paul Ehrlich and John Holdren; Commoner blamed production technology, Ehrlich and Holdren stressed population growth.
Affluence is average consumption per person, often proxied by GDP per capita; technology measures how resource-intensive that affluence is, such as emissions per unit of GDP.
Impact can be measured in global hectares with ecological footprint analysis; if it exceeds carrying capacity the system is in overshoot.
The Kaya identity is a similar formula applied specifically to carbon dioxide emissions.
Critics say P, A and T are not independent: halving T may not halve impact if cheaper use stimulates more consumption, the rebound effect.
It is also faulted for ignoring political context and for blaming the global poor.
It underpins the World3 simulation model.

contested_note: Environmentalists debate whether impact can be written as a simple product of independent factors and which factors matter most.

title: Khazzoom–Brookes postulate

definition.text: The claim that energy-efficiency improvements that make sense for individual users lead to higher total energy use across the economy.

facts.text: Economists Daniel Khazzoom and Leonard Brookes put forward the idea independently in the 1980s; Harry Saunders named it in 1992 and showed it holds in neoclassical growth theory under many assumptions.
Efficiency raises energy use by making energy cheaper, by speeding economic growth, and by unlocking other activities that a scarce resource had held back.
After the 1973 and 1979 oil crises cars became more fuel-efficient on average, yet total consumption kept rising.
It is a modern version of the Jevons paradox.

contested_note: Economists debate whether the postulate is correct and how much it matters for energy policy.
